1. Meaning of Militant Nationalism

  • Militant nationalism represented strands of the freedom struggle that believed British rule could require direct confrontation, underground organisation or armed resistance.
  • It developed alongside constitutional nationalism and Gandhian non-violence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Militant Nationalism → Direct Action + Revolutionary Organisation + Armed Resistance

2. Revolutionary Nationalism

  • Revolutionary nationalists attempted to overthrow colonial rule through organised political action outside normal constitutional channels.

Some groups used:

  • Secret societies.
  • Arms.
  • Bombs.
  • Political assassinations.
  • Military organisation.

3. Main Objective

  • Their ultimate objective was the end of British rule and establishment of an independent India.

4. Difference from Assertive Nationalism

Assertive nationalists such as Tilak emphasised:

  • Swadeshi.
  • Boycott.
  • Mass mobilisation.

Revolutionary nationalists could additionally use:

  • Secret organisation.
  • Armed action.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Tilak's Assertive Nationalism ≠ Secret Revolutionary Terrorism

5. Difference from Satyagraha

Satyagraha:

  • Non-violent.
  • Open.
  • Acceptance of punishment.

Militant revolutionary action:

  • Could be secret.
  • Could involve weapons.
  • Could seek to overthrow colonial power by force.

Important centres of revolutionary nationalism included:

  • Bengal.
  • Maharashtra.
  • Punjab.
  • London.
  • North India.
  • Tamil Nadu.
  • Overseas Indian communities.

216. Date

  • The Provisional Government was proclaimed on 21 October 1943.

  • "Delhi Chalo" became a famous INA mobilisation call.

  • "Jai Hind" became strongly associated with the INA and Subhas Bose.

222. Women and Armed Nationalism

  • The regiment became an important symbol of women's participation in militant anti-colonial nationalism.

223. Andaman and Nicobar Islands

  • Japan transferred nominal control of the Andaman and Nicobar Islands to the Azad Hind Government.

226. Imphal

227. Kohima

  • The wider Japanese advance also produced the Battle of Kohima.

228. 1944 Campaign

  • The Imphal–Kohima campaign occurred in 1944.

229. Failure

The offensive failed because of:

  • Strong Allied resistance.
  • Severe supply difficulties.
  • Monsoon conditions.
  • Japanese military reverses.

230. INA Retreat

  • INA forces retreated with the Japanese.

231. Japan Surrenders

  • Japan surrendered in August 1945.

232. Collapse of INA Military Campaign

  • Japan's defeat ended the INA's ability to continue large-scale military operations.

233. INA Prisoners

  • Many INA officers and soldiers were captured by British forces.

234. INA Trials

  • British authorities tried selected INA officers at the Red Fort in Delhi.

236. Religious Diversity

  • The three defendants represented different religious communities.
  • Their joint trial strengthened the image of national unity.

237. Defence

  • Prominent Indian lawyers and political leaders participated in the legal defence.

238. Jawaharlal Nehru

  • Jawaharlal Nehru appeared in legal robes in support of the INA defence effort.

239. Mass Sympathy

  • The INA trials generated enormous public sympathy across India.

240. Congress and INA

  • Congress had major ideological differences with Bose's wartime methods, but it strongly opposed colonial punishment of INA soldiers.

241. Political Effect

  • The INA trials weakened British confidence that Indian armed personnel could remain insulated from nationalism.

  • The Royal Indian Navy uprising occurred in February 1946.

243. Bombay

  • Bombay became the main centre of the naval uprising.

244. Ratings

  • Indian naval ratings protested against:
    • Poor conditions.
    • Racial discrimination.
    • Unsatisfactory treatment.

245. Political Demands

  • Wider nationalist and anti-colonial demands also appeared during the uprising.

246. Spread

  • The unrest spread to several naval establishments.

247. Civilian Support

  • Workers and civilians in Bombay expressed solidarity.

248. Importance

  • The RIN uprising demonstrated serious political unrest inside the colonial armed forces shortly before independence.

  • The INA trials and RIN uprising contributed to the late-colonial crisis of military loyalty.

1945–46 → INA Trials + RIN Uprising → Colonial Military Confidence Weakened

250. Revolutionary vs Military Movement

  • Early revolutionary groups operated mainly through small underground cells.
  • INA represented organised military resistance on a much larger scale.

251. Evolution of Militancy

The broad sequence was:

Secret societies → Political assassinations → Overseas conspiracy → Organised revolutionary republicans → Socialist revolutionary groups → Guerrilla raids → Overseas army.

Bengal is especially associated with:

  • Anushilan Samiti.
  • Jugantar.
  • Muzaffarpur.
  • Alipore.
  • Chittagong.

253. Maharashtra Contribution

  • Abhinav Bharat.
  • Nashik conspiracy.

  • Komagata Maru.

  • Azad Hind Fauj.

258. Women in Revolutionary Movements

Important women included:

  • Pritilata Waddedar.
  • Kalpana Datta.
  • Lakshmi Sahgal.

259. Revolutionary Martyrdom

  • Executions often increased public admiration for revolutionaries rather than ending nationalist sentiment.

260. Youth Appeal

  • Revolutionary movements were particularly attractive to sections of nationalist youth frustrated with gradual political methods.

261. Sacrifice

  • Revolutionary literature emphasised:
    • Courage.
    • Self-sacrifice.
    • Patriotism.
    • Fearlessness.

262. Limitations

  • Small underground groups found it difficult to organise a sustained nationwide armed uprising.

263. Intelligence Penetration

  • Informers and colonial intelligence frequently disrupted revolutionary plans.

264. Arms Problem

  • Access to:
    • Weapons.
    • Ammunition.
    • Funds was a persistent limitation.

265. Limited Mass Base

  • Many early revolutionary organisations had smaller mass bases than Gandhian movements.

266. Colonial Repression

British methods included:

  • Surveillance.
  • Arrest.
  • Deportation.
  • Special tribunals.
  • Executions.
  • Transportation.

267. Cellular Jail

  • Transportation to the Andaman Cellular Jail became a major punishment for revolutionaries.

268. Ideological Evolution

  • Revolutionary nationalism changed over time.
  • Early groups frequently emphasised individual heroic action.
  • Later organisations such as HSRA increasingly discussed socialism and mass revolution.

269. Hindu-Muslim Unity

  • Revolutionary organisations often contained activists from multiple religious communities.

Examples:

  • Bismil + Ashfaqulla.
  • Bhagat Singh's HSRA circle.
  • INA trial defendants.

270. Nationalism Beyond Religion

  • Revolutionary nationalism frequently presented independence as a common political cause transcending religion.
Boundary

Detailed rise of communal politics → Chapter 30.

271. Revolutionary Nationalism and Congress

  • Relations with Congress varied.
  • Revolutionary groups often criticised Congress methods.
  • Congress nevertheless defended civil liberties and sometimes supported imprisoned revolutionaries politically.

272. Gandhi and Revolutionaries

  • Gandhi disagreed fundamentally with political violence.
  • However, revolutionary martyrs could still command enormous popular respect.

273. Bhagat Singh's Popularity

  • Bhagat Singh became a national icon extending far beyond the membership of HSRA.

274. INA Popularity

  • INA soldiers became symbols of patriotic sacrifice despite disagreement over Bose's international alliances.

275. Political vs Military Success

  • Many militant campaigns failed to defeat Britain militarily.
  • Their political impact was nevertheless substantial.

276. Main Political Effects

They:

  • Inspired nationalist youth.
  • Challenged colonial authority.
  • Created martyrs.
  • Internationalised Indian independence.
  • Raised doubts about military loyalty.
